medium.titulo: NVIDIA Neotron 3 Ultra AI & Autonomous Software Engineering
medium.resumo: Building Apps Without Writing Code: How NVIDIA Neotron 3 Ultra Is Pushing AI Toward Autonomous Software Engineering
medium.conteudo_html:
Building Apps Without Writing Code: How NVIDIA Neotron 3 Ultra Is Pushing AI Toward Autonomous Software Engineering

What if you could describe an application in plain English — and an AI agent could design it, write the code, test it, find its own mistakes, fix them, and deliver a working application?

That is the promise behind NVIDIA Neotron 3 Ultra, a massive 550-billion-parameter AI model designed to push the boundaries of reasoning and autonomous software development.

Combined with local AI tooling such as Ollama, this approach points toward a future where building software may require far less traditional coding.

From Coding Assistant to Software Engineer

Traditional AI coding assistants typically work like this:

  1. You describe what you want.
  2. The AI generates code.
  3. You run the code.
  4. You find an error.
  5. You return to the AI for a fix.
  6. The process repeats.

The interesting shift with Neotron 3 Ultra is the emphasis on self-correction.

Instead of simply generating code and waiting for the developer to discover problems, the model can reason through its output, identify issues, make corrections, and continue toward a working result.

That changes the role of the AI.

It is no longer simply answering:

“What code should I write?”

It is moving toward:

“How do I build the complete solution?”

The EMI Calculator Experiment

One particularly interesting example is an AI agent being asked to build a functional EMI calculator from scratch.

The requirement sounds relatively simple: calculate loan repayments.

But a useful application needs much more than a mathematical formula.

The AI produced an application containing elements such as:

  • Interactive loan parameters
  • Functional sliders
  • EMI calculations
  • Repayment information
  • Long-term repayment visualization
  • A 20-year repayment chart
  • User-interface components
  • Working application logic

The important part wasn’t simply that the AI generated the code.

It Checked Its Own Work

The model used a self-correction process to examine its output.

If it encountered an error or something that didn’t work as expected, it could reason about the problem and modify its implementation rather than immediately requiring another instruction from the user.

That creates a development loop resembling:

Requirement → Generate → Test → Detect Error → Correct → Test Again → Deliver

This is fundamentally different from one-shot code generation.

What Makes This Important?

The biggest change isn’t the number of parameters.

It’s the workflow.

For years, AI-assisted programming has primarily focused on making developers faster.

Tools could:

  • Generate functions
  • Explain code
  • Fix bugs
  • Write tests
  • Convert between programming languages
  • Suggest implementations

Agentic AI takes another step.

Instead of waiting for instructions after every operation, an agent can potentially coordinate multiple stages of development on its own.

That means the developer moves from being the person writing every line of code toward being the person defining the requirements, constraints, architecture, and acceptance criteria.

Ollama Makes Local AI More Interesting

A major part of this trend is the growth of local AI infrastructure.

Tools such as Ollama make it easier to run supported AI models locally and connect them to development workflows.

The basic concept is straightforward:

AI Model + Local Runtime + Agent + Development Tools = Local Autonomous Coding Environment

Instead of sending every piece of source code to a cloud API, developers can increasingly experiment with models running within their own infrastructure — where hardware and model requirements permit it.

For companies working with sensitive source code, proprietary algorithms, infrastructure software, or regulated workloads, local execution can be particularly interesting.

Could This Replace SaaS Tools?

This is where the implications become much larger.

Consider a company that needs a simple internal application:

  • EMI calculator
  • Pricing calculator
  • Capacity planner
  • Resource estimator
  • Deployment dashboard
  • Log-analysis utility
  • Configuration generator
  • Internal reporting tool

Historically, the choices might have been:

Buy SaaS → Build internally → Hire developers → Use spreadsheets

Agentic AI introduces another option:

Describe the tool → Let the AI build it → Review and deploy

For relatively small and well-defined applications, the economics could change significantly.

Instead of paying for a specialized SaaS subscription indefinitely, an organization could potentially generate a custom internal tool tailored to its exact requirements.

But “No-Code” Doesn’t Mean “No Engineering”

There is an important distinction here.

AI-generated software still needs engineering discipline.

A model can generate an impressive application while introducing problems involving:

  • Security
  • Authentication
  • Authorization
  • Data validation
  • Dependency vulnerabilities
  • Performance
  • Reliability
  • Maintainability
  • Incorrect business logic
  • Privacy
  • Compliance

A working demo is not automatically a production-ready system.

For example, an EMI calculator can produce the correct-looking UI while still containing subtle calculation or rounding errors.

The same principle becomes much more important when AI generates systems handling financial transactions, customer information, infrastructure, or security-sensitive operations.

The Developer’s Role Is Changing

The most interesting consequence may not be that programmers disappear.

Instead, the definition of programming may change.

The traditional workflow is:

Human → Code → Compiler → Application

The emerging workflow looks more like:

Human → Requirements → AI Agent → Code/Test/Debug → Application

The human increasingly becomes responsible for:

  • Defining requirements
  • Setting constraints
  • Reviewing architecture
  • Validating behavior
  • Managing security
  • Testing critical paths
  • Making engineering trade-offs

The AI handles more of the mechanical implementation.

From Copilot to Autonomous Engineer

This represents an important progression in AI-assisted development.

Generation

AI writes code based on a prompt.

Assistance

AI helps developers complete tasks, debug problems, and understand unfamiliar code.

Agentic Development

AI plans multiple steps, uses tools, executes code, observes results, and iterates.

Autonomous Software Engineering

AI increasingly owns the loop:

Plan → Implement → Execute → Evaluate → Correct → Repeat

The EMI calculator example demonstrates why that final stage is so compelling.

The breakthrough isn’t merely that AI can write a calculator.

Developers have been generating calculators with AI for years.

The breakthrough is the possibility of an AI system that can take responsibility for the development loop rather than just producing a code snippet.

What This Could Mean for Enterprise Software

For enterprise engineering teams, the opportunity is potentially much broader than building small utilities.

Agentic development could eventually assist with:

  • Internal developer tools
  • Automation scripts
  • Test frameworks
  • CI/CD tooling
  • Monitoring utilities
  • Data-processing pipelines
  • API integrations
  • Migration tooling
  • Infrastructure automation
  • Prototype applications

The strongest use cases are likely to be systems where requirements are well defined and the AI has access to reliable testing and validation mechanisms.

That’s because self-correction works best when the agent has a way to observe whether its changes actually worked.

The Real Breakthrough: Closing the Feedback Loop

The most important concept here isn’t “550 billion parameters.”

It’s the feedback loop.

A conventional LLM produces an answer.

An agent can potentially:

  1. Produce an implementation.
  2. Run it.
  3. Observe the result.
  4. Compare the result against expectations.
  5. Diagnose failures.
  6. Modify the implementation.
  7. Run it again.

That feedback loop is what transforms AI from a code generator into something much closer to an engineering system.

The Bigger Picture

The long-term impact of models such as Neotron 3 Ultra may therefore extend beyond faster programming.

The bigger question is:

What happens when software itself becomes something you can generate on demand?

Instead of searching for an existing application that fits your workflow, you could describe the workflow and generate an application specifically for it.

Instead of adapting your business process to SaaS software, you could potentially adapt software to your business process.

And instead of spending days building a small internal tool, an AI agent could potentially handle much of the implementation work in a single session.

Final Takeaway

AI coding is evolving from autocomplete to autonomous software engineering.

The significance of Neotron 3 Ultra isn’t simply its enormous parameter count. The more interesting development is the combination of large-scale reasoning, local execution, tool use, and self-correction.

The future may not be completely “no-code.”

It may be something more powerful:

Less code written by humans, more software engineered through human intent.

The developer doesn’t disappear.

The developer moves up the abstraction stack — from writing every line of code to defining what the software should accomplish.

medium.titulo: The 63% Rule: Designing Agents Humans Actually Trust With Autonomy
medium.resumo: The problem nobody wants to name
medium.conteudo_html:
The problem nobody wants to name

Ask a team running an AI agent in production what percentage of its actions execute without a human in the loop. Most cannot answer. They track latency, token spend, task success. But the number that decides whether the project survives, the autonomy rate, goes unmeasured.

Then the arc plays out the way it always does. The demo is magic. The pilot is promising. The agent gets real tools and real consequences, and within weeks someone asks the question that kills the project: “Can we have it ask before doing that?”

Then it asks before doing everything. The agent becomes a chatbot with extra steps, the team stops using it, and the project quietly dies. Your agent does not have a trust problem. It has an autonomy calibration problem.

The industry’s default answer is “human in the loop,” which usually means a human rubber-stamping every action until they stop reading and click approve on muscle memory. That is not safety. That is liability with extra latency.

What actually works is calibrated autonomy: a deliberate split between what the agent does alone and what it escalates, with the split itself treated as a metric you manage.

TL;DR

  • Most agent projects die from autonomy miscalibration, not capability gaps: too much freedom causes an incident, too little turns the agent into a chatbot.
  • The 63% Rule: aim for roughly 60 to 65% of actions executing without human confirmation. Gate the rest by reversibility and blast radius. Block the dangerous few entirely.
  • Implement it as deterministic policy code, not prompts. Measure autonomy rate and override rate weekly. Widen autonomy only on evidence.

The 63% Rule, stated plainly

The 63% Rule is a practitioner’s heuristic, not a peer-reviewed finding. The number is deliberately specific and deliberately unofficial. Nothing in this article depends on the number being exactly right.

It goes like this: in a healthy production deployment, roughly 60 to 65 percent of an agent’s actions should execute without human confirmation. The rest get escalated, gated, or blocked. If your autonomy rate is much higher, you are almost certainly under-gated and one bad afternoon away from an incident. If it is much lower, you have built an expensive suggestion engine and your operators will route around it.

Why 63 and not 50 or 80? Because the natural shape of real work is that about two thirds of actions are routine, reversible, and low blast radius: lookups, drafts, reschedules, summaries. The remaining third is where the risk lives: money moving, permissions changing, messages sent externally, state deleted. The rule just names the split that reality keeps producing. (If 63% reminds you of 1 minus 1/e, that is a coincidence, not a derivation.)

The point of the number is not precision. The point is that autonomy rate is a metric you should be measuring and managing, with a target band, the same way you manage latency or error budgets. Most teams cannot tell you their agent’s autonomy rate. That is the actual problem. Trust is not a feeling. It is a metric with a target band.

What calibrated autonomy actually does

Calibrated autonomy runs every proposed action through a risk gate before execution. The gate answers three questions:

  • Is this action reversible? A draft can be discarded. A sent email cannot be unsent. A refund can be re-charged, awkwardly. A deleted database only comes back from a restore.
  • What is the blast radius? One record versus ten thousand. Internal versus customer-facing. Read versus write.
  • How confident are we in the classification? The gate itself can be wrong, so high-stakes actions need deterministic rules, not vibes.

Based on those answers, each action lands in one of three tiers:

  • Auto (the 63%): executes immediately, fully logged. Read-only operations, drafts, notifications, reschedules, anything reversible with narrow blast radius.
  • Gated (most of the 37%): pauses for human approval with full context. Money movement above a threshold, external communication, permission changes, bulk operations.
  • Blocked: never executes via the agent, no matter what. Credential rotation, data deletion beyond soft-delete, legal or compliance attestations. These stay human-only by policy, not by prompt.

The critical insight: the tiers are not fixed. They are the output of a policy you version and adjust based on measured override rates. When humans approve 98% of gated sub-$50 refunds for weeks, that boundary is wrong and you move it. The 63% is a starting target, not a permanent address.

Architecture: the autonomy gate

The pipeline every production agent needs, whatever you build it with:

User request / trigger
        |
        v
+------------------+
|  Planner (LLM)   |  proposes a plan: sequence of tool calls
+------------------+
        |
        v
+------------------+
| Action classifier|  deterministic rules first, model judgment
| (risk scoring)   |  only for the ambiguous remainder
+------------------+
        |
        v
+------------------+
|   Policy gate    |  OPA-style rules: allow / gate / block
|  (deterministic)|  versioned, audited, tested in CI
+------------------+
        |
   +----+----+------------------+
   |         |                  |
   v         v                  v
 AUTO      GATED              BLOCKED
 executes  interrupt:         rejected,
 logs      human approves      logged with
           or rejects          reason
   |         |
   v         v
+------------------+
|  Audit log +     |  every action, decision, latency,
|  trace (OTel)    |  override, and outcome recorded
+------------------+
        |
        v
+------------------+
| Autonomy metrics |  autonomy rate, override rate,
| dashboard        |  escalation precision, incidents
+------------------+

Two design decisions matter most here.

First, the policy gate is deterministic code, not a prompt. Prompts are for judgment; policy is for guarantees. “Refunds over $500 require approval” should be a rule evaluated by code, the same way your API gateway enforces auth. If your safety boundary lives inside a system prompt, you do not have a safety boundary. You have a suggestion.

Second, the classifier may say “I don’t know,” and that routes to Gated. Most incidents come from confident misclassifications, not known risks. An explicit low-confidence path converts unknown unknowns into human decisions.

Implementation

Let us make this concrete. The scenario: a support-ops agent for an e-commerce company with a handful of tools. Everything below is real, runnable Python using Pydantic for validation and LangGraph’s human-in-the-loop primitives for escalation.

Step 1: Classify actions with Pydantic, not vibes

from enum import Enum
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
class RiskTier(str, Enum):
    AUTO = "auto"        # executes immediately
    GATED = "gated"      # needs human approval
    BLOCKED = "blocked"  # never via agent
class AgentAction(BaseModel):
    name: str
    args: dict = Field(default_factory=dict)
    # "reversible" | "partially" | "irreversible"
    reversibility: str
    # "single" | "bulk" | "external"
    blast_radius: str
# Deterministic policy table. Version this. Review it monthly.
# This is the actual safety boundary, keep it out of prompts.
POLICY = {
    # (tool, condition) -> tier
    ("lookup_order", None): RiskTier.AUTO,
    ("draft_reply", None): RiskTier.AUTO,
    ("reschedule_delivery", None): RiskTier.AUTO,
    ("issue_refund", "amount <= 50"): RiskTier.AUTO,
    ("issue_refund", "amount > 50"): RiskTier.GATED,
    ("send_customer_email", None): RiskTier.GATED,
    ("ban_account", None): RiskTier.BLOCKED,
    ("delete_order_history", None): RiskTier.BLOCKED,
}
def classify(action: AgentAction) -> RiskTier:
    """Deterministic classification. No LLM involved."""
    key = (action.name, None)
    if action.name == "issue_refund":
        amount = action.args.get("amount_usd", 0)
        if amount <= 50:
            key = (action.name, "amount <= 50")
        else:
            key = (action.name, "amount > 50")
    tier = POLICY.get(key)
    if tier is None:
        # Unknown action: escalate, never auto-run.
        return RiskTier.GATED
    # Defense in depth: irreversible + external is never AUTO,
    # even if the table says so. Guards against misconfiguration.
    risky = (action.reversibility == "irreversible"
             and action.blast_radius == "external")
    if risky and tier == RiskTier.AUTO:
        return RiskTier.GATED
    return tier

Two properties make this production-grade: unknown actions default to Gated, never Auto, and a defense-in-depth override stops a misconfigured table from auto-approving anything irreversible and external. Design as if your policy table already has bugs.

Step 2: Gate execution with a real human-in-the-loop interrupt

LangGraph ships a first-class human-in-the-loop primitive: interrupt(), which pauses graph execution mid-node and resumes when a human responds. This is the correct mechanism for the Gated tier, far better than "the agent asks in chat and hopes."

from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END
from langgraph.types import interrupt, Command
from langgraph.checkpoint import MemorySaver
from typing import TypedDict

class AgentState(TypedDict):
    # the proposed AgentAction, as a dict
    action: dict
    approved: bool
    result: dict

def policy_gate(state: AgentState) -> dict:
    action = AgentAction(**state["action"])
    tier = classify(action)

    if tier == RiskTier.BLOCKED:
        reason = f"{action.name} is blocked by policy"
        result = {"status": "blocked", "reason": reason}
        return {"approved": False, "result": result}

    if tier == RiskTier.GATED:
        # Execution PAUSES here. A human reviews the full
        # action context, then replies approve or reject.
        decision = interrupt({
            "question": f"Approve {action.name}?",
            "action": action.model_dump(),
            "tier": "gated",
        })
        approved = decision.get("verdict") == "approve"
        note = decision.get("note", "")
        result = {"reviewer_note": note}
        return {"approved": approved, "result": result}

    # AUTO tier: no pause, executes immediately.
    return {"approved": True}

def execute(state: AgentState) -> dict:
    if not state["approved"]:
        result = {**state["result"], "executed": False}
        return {"result": result}
    # Call the real tool here.
    # Always use idempotency keys and timeouts.
    tool_name = state["action"]["name"]
    result = {"executed": True, "tool": tool_name}
    return {"result": result}

graph = StateGraph(AgentState)
graph.add_node("policy_gate", policy_gate)
graph.add_node("execute", execute)
graph.add_edge(START, "policy_gate")
graph.add_edge("policy_gate", "execute")
graph.add_edge("execute", END)
app = graph.compile(checkpointer=MemorySaver())

# Resuming after a human decision:
# resume = {"verdict": "approve", "note": "verified"}
# cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "abc123"}}
# app.invoke(Command(resume=resume), config=cfg)

The interrupt carries full action context to the reviewer, and the pause is durable. If the reviewer goes to lunch, the action waits. Compare that to the anti-pattern where the agent “asks” in the chat transcript and proceeds on a timeout. Timeouts are how incidents happen.

Step 3: Measure the autonomy rate

You cannot manage what you do not measure. Every action, gate decision, and human override goes to the audit log, and a small job computes the metrics that actually run the system:

def autonomy_report(actions: list[dict]) -> dict:
    """Build from audit log entries.

    Each entry has: tier ("auto" / "gated" / "blocked")
    and human_overridden (bool).
    """
    total = len(actions)
    auto = sum(1 for a in actions if a["tier"] == "auto")
    gated = sum(1 for a in actions if a["tier"] == "gated")
    overrides = sum(1 for a in actions
                    if a.get("human_overridden"))

    # Target band for autonomy_rate: 0.60 to 0.65.
    autonomy_rate = round(auto / total, 3)
    gated_rate = round(gated / total, 3)
    override_rate = round(overrides / max(gated, 1), 3)

    # How to read override_rate (illustrative, tune it):
    #   below 0.05 -> boundary too conservative, widen AUTO
    #   above 0.25 -> gate catches real mistakes, do NOT widen
    return {
        "autonomy_rate": autonomy_rate,
        "gated_rate": gated_rate,
        "override_rate": override_rate,
    }

The override rate is the most important number in production agent operations. A gate nobody ever overrides is either perfect or, far more likely, being rubber-stamped. Tune the policy table against this number monthly.

Where the AI actually goes (and where it does not)

A common mistake is putting the LLM in charge of the safety decision. Here is the correct division of labor:

Deterministic code handles: tier classification for known actions, threshold checks, allowlists and blocklists, idempotency, timeouts, retries, audit logging. These are guarantees, and guarantees do not come from next-token prediction.

The LLM handles: planning (which actions to propose), drafting content for human review, summarizing context for the approver, and classifying novel actions with an explicit confidence score. Anything below your confidence threshold routes to Gated automatically.

The human handles: approving gated actions, reviewing policy, investigating overrides. Notice what the human does not do: read every auto-tier action. That is the 63% paying off. Human attention is the scarcest resource in the system; spend it where the risk is.

The model’s input is the proposed action plus context; its output is a proposed tier with a confidence score and one-line rationale for the reviewer. Model confidence is not calibrated probability. Treat it as a triage signal, never a safety guarantee; the deterministic rules are the guarantee.

Practical example: the support-ops agent, week one versus week eight

Consider the support agent above, handling roughly 1,000 actions per week. All numbers below are illustrative, not measured results. They show the shape of a healthy calibration curve, not a benchmark.

Week one (conservative start):

  • Autonomy rate: 41%. Everything ambiguous starts Gated.
  • Gated actions: 590, humans approved 96%.
  • Override rate: 4%. The gate is catching almost nothing, so it is too tight.
  • Operator feedback: “I am just clicking approve all day.”

The calibration move: refunds under $50 move from Gated to Auto. Policy table gets a version bump and changelog entry.

Week eight (calibrated):

  • Autonomy rate: 63%. Lookups, sub-$50 refunds, reschedules, and drafts run free.
  • Gated actions: 340 per week, mostly larger refunds and outbound emails.
  • Override rate: 11%. The gate now catches real mistakes at a meaningful rate.
  • Incidents: zero customer-facing errors from auto-tier actions.
  • Approval time down roughly 60%, and reviewers report actually reading gated items again.

That last point is the one nobody talks about. Approval fatigue is a safety vulnerability. A human asked to approve 600 near-identical actions a week stops reading them by Wednesday. Fewer, better-targeted interruptions produce better human decisions on the ones that remain. The 37% exists to protect the quality of human judgment, not just to catch agent mistakes.

Results and evaluation: what to actually measure

Forget “task success rate.” For autonomy calibration, the metrics that matter are:

  • Autonomy rate: fraction of actions executing without human confirmation. Target band 0.60 to 0.65 for most deployments. Below 0.5, you have a chatbot. Above 0.8, you have an incident waiting for a trigger.
  • Override rate: fraction of gated actions the human rejects or modifies. Healthy range is roughly 0.05 to 0.25. Below that, widen autonomy. Above that, hold or tighten.
  • Escalation precision: of escalated actions, how many actually needed a human? Low precision means a noisy classifier and reviewers who stop trusting the queue.
  • Time-to-decision on gated actions: p50 and p95. If p95 approval latency is 4 hours, your “real-time” agent is a batch process.
  • Incident rate per 1,000 auto-tier actions: the number that justifies the entire apparatus. Any upward trend means the Auto tier boundary is wrong.

Run these as a weekly report and a monthly policy review. The moment you treat the autonomy split as “configured once,” you have stopped operating the system.

Limitations and failure modes

This framework fails in specific, predictable ways. Know them first.

The classifier is the new attack surface. Prompt injection only needs to make a dangerous action look low-risk. Mitigation: classify on structured action schemas (tool name, typed args), never on natural-language descriptions, and treat tool outputs as untrusted data, always.

Distributional shift eats static policies. The table that was correct in March is wrong in June. Calendar a monthly review and trigger an automatic one whenever a new tool is registered or an incident occurs.

The 63% is a heuristic, and heuristics have jurisdictions. A support agent and a production-database agent should not share a target band. For irreversible, regulated, or safety-critical domains, start far lower, think 20 to 30%, and earn upward slowly. The rule tells you to manage the number, not what the number must be.

Humans habituate. Rubber-stamping is the failure mode of every approval queue. Countermeasures that work: show reviewers the rationale and blast radius, not just an approve button; rotate reviewers; sample auto-tier actions for retroactive review.

Correlated failures. A systematic blind spot misclassifies the same way a thousand times before anyone notices. That is why the audit log and incident-rate metric exist: the metrics are the second gate.

Production considerations

A few things that separate a demo of this architecture from a production deployment of it:

  • Observability: trace every action with OpenTelemetry, plus LangSmith or Langfuse for planning traces. At 2 AM you need the full chain: what the agent saw, proposed, what the gate decided, who approved it.
  • Policy as code: the policy table lives in version control, changes go through review, and tests assert that known-dangerous actions classify as Blocked. If you cannot write a test for your safety boundary, you do not have one.
  • Kill switches and rate limits: a global kill switch that drops everything to manual, per-tool rate limits, and circuit breakers that auto-tighten policy when incident rate spikes. The system must fail toward less autonomy, never more.
  • Idempotency: every mutating tool call carries an idempotency key. Retries after a gate timeout must not double-execute. Unglamorous and non-negotiable.
  • Secrets and PII: tools run under least-privilege credentials, PII is redacted from traces by default, and the review UI shows only the minimum context needed.
  • Red-teaming: before raising autonomy, adversarially test the classifier with prompt-injected tool outputs. The gate eval suite (Ragas, DeepEval, or hand-rolled) runs in CI, not in a one-off notebook.
  • Incident runbooks: decide in advance what happens when an auto-tier action causes harm: who gets paged, how it is reversed, how the policy gets patched. The first incident is not the time to design this.

Practical recommendations

If you are building or operating an agent, here is the sequence:

  1. Inventory every tool the agent can call and label each with reversibility and blast radius. This takes an afternoon and is the highest-value exercise in this article.
  2. Write the policy table as code, with tests, before the agent ships. Start conservative: when in doubt, Gate it.
  3. Ship with full audit logging from day one. You cannot calibrate later what you did not record now.
  4. Measure autonomy rate and override rate weekly. Set the target band (start at 0.60 to 0.65 unless your domain says otherwise) and review monthly.
  5. Widen autonomy only on evidence: sustained low override rates, zero incidents, reviewers confirming the gated queue still gets real attention.
  6. Never let the model set policy. It proposes, classifies with confidence, and drafts. Deterministic code decides.
  7. Run a monthly policy review with the incident log open. The split is a living configuration, not a launch setting.

Conclusion

The agents that earn trust are not the most capable ones. They are the ones whose operators can say, at any moment, exactly what the agent may do alone, what it must ask about, and what it can never touch, and show the numbers proving the split works.

The 63% Rule is a memorable way to say: manage autonomy like a metric, gate on reversibility and blast radius, keep policy in deterministic code, and spend human attention where the risk lives. Do that, and your agent keeps its autonomy. Skip it, and you get the demo, the pilot, and then the meeting where someone asks if it can just ask before doing that.

FAQ

Is 63% a real measured number?
No. It is a practitioner’s heuristic: roughly two thirds of actions autonomous, one third gated or blocked. Treat it as a starting target band to calibrate from, not a law.

Does this apply to coding agents?
Yes: Auto for test runs, linting, and local edits; Gated for pushes, merges, and deployments; Blocked for production database writes and secret rotation.

What about fully autonomous agents with no humans?
Then you have implicitly set autonomy to 100% with no calibration signal at all. At minimum, keep the audit log and the incident-rate metric. You are flying without instruments otherwise.

Which framework should I use?
The pattern is framework-agnostic. LangGraph’s interrupt() is the cleanest human-in-the-loop primitive I have used; Temporal is excellent for durable execution; a hand-rolled gate with Pydantic and a review queue is perfectly respectable for v1. Pick the one your team will actually operate.

Build checklist

  • Tool inventory with reversibility and blast radius labels
  • Policy table as versioned code, with tests for Blocked actions
  • Deterministic classifier with unknown-defaults-to-Gated
  • Human approval UI showing full action context, rationale, and blast radius
  • Durable interrupts (no timeout-proceeds)
  • Full audit log: proposed action, tier, decision, latency, outcome
  • Weekly autonomy rate and override rate report
  • Monthly policy review cadence
  • Kill switch, rate limits, circuit breakers
  • Idempotency keys on all mutating tools
  • Red-team eval suite for the classifier, running in CI
  • Incident runbook with reversal procedures

medium.conteudo_html:
AI has changed the cost and speed of building software. A product that once required a developer, a designer, a backend engineer, a few weeks of work, and a lot of patience can now be turned into a working prototype with a conversation, a good prompt, and an AI coding tool. That is an incredible shift, but there is a problem hiding underneath it. Getting software to work is not the same thing as building software that can survive.

The original article that inspired this piece makes that problem especially clear through the story of a founder who built a full stack SaaS product over a weekend with Cursor, only to have the database lock up shortly after launch. The broader argument is that AI has made software creation dramatically easier, but it has not removed the engineering problems that appear once real users, real traffic, real data, and real money enter the picture. Medium

https://t.me/aicoursesdaily

AI Made Building Software Almost Too Easy

There was a time when building even a basic SaaS product required a fairly serious technical commitment. Someone had to understand the frontend, backend, database, authentication, payments, deployment, security, monitoring, and everything else that sits between an idea and a functioning product. Today, much of that work can be described in ordinary language and handed to an AI coding assistant.

That change is genuinely exciting. A founder can describe a product idea, generate a user interface, connect an API, create database models, add authentication, integrate payments, deploy the application, and start showing it to customers without spending months writing everything manually. Tools such as Cursor and other AI powered development environments have made the first version of an idea dramatically cheaper to produce.

The danger is that the first version can look much more complete than it actually is.

A polished interface can create the impression that the difficult work is finished. The buttons work. The login page looks professional. Payments go through. The dashboard loads. A few people use the product and everything appears fine. From the outside, it looks like a real company has been built.

Underneath that interface, however, there may be decisions that nobody has properly examined.

An MVP Is Not Supposed to Be Perfect

There is nothing wrong with taking shortcuts during the early stages of a product. In fact, that is often exactly what an MVP is for. The purpose is to test whether people actually want the product before investing heavily in infrastructure, engineering, design, and operations.

Technical debt is easy to ignore when everything is moving quickly. The product is still changing, users are still arriving, and there is always something more urgent than cleaning up code that appears to be working. An MVP is supposed to be simple, so taking a few shortcuts can be perfectly reasonable at that stage. The problem starts when those temporary decisions quietly become permanent parts of the system.

That distinction matters.

There is a huge difference between deliberately building a simple system because the business has not validated its assumptions and accidentally building a fragile system because nobody understood what the AI generated.

One is a product decision. The other is an engineering problem.

The First Few Users Can Be Misleading

Early traction can hide a surprising number of problems.

A product with ten users might work perfectly even when the architecture is poorly designed. A database query that is inefficient with a million records can still feel instant when there are only a few hundred. A background job that would collapse under heavy traffic might appear completely reliable when it only runs twenty times a day.

That is why the early stage can be deceptive.

Everything feels fast because there is almost no pressure on the system. Then the product starts getting attention. More users arrive. More data accumulates. More requests hit the API. Payment events increase. Background jobs begin running simultaneously. Suddenly, the assumptions made during the weekend prototype become production problems.

This is where software engineering becomes much more than writing code.

The real question is no longer whether the application works. It becomes whether the application continues to work when reality stops being predictable.

AI Is Very Good at the Happy Path

One of the easiest ways to understand the limitation is to look at the happy path.

Tell an AI to build a signup system and it can probably create one quickly. Ask for authentication, database integration, password reset functionality, and an attractive login page, and the result may look surprisingly good.

Real users, however, do not follow the happy path.

They forget passwords. They refresh pages halfway through a transaction. They submit forms twice. Their internet connection disappears. They open the same account on multiple devices. They upload unexpected files. Payments fail. Webhooks arrive late. Third party APIs return strange responses. Databases become unavailable. Two processes attempt to modify the same record at almost the same time.

These are not unusual edge cases. They are part of running software in the real world.

AI can help engineers think through these situations, generate tests, identify possible failures, and implement fixes. But someone still needs to understand which failures matter, how the system should behave, and whether the proposed solution is actually safe.

That responsibility does not disappear because the code was generated.

The Hidden Cost of AI Generated Software

The most expensive part of AI generated software may not be the first version.

The first version can be incredibly cheap.

The expensive part can arrive later when another developer has to understand it.

Imagine a startup that grows quickly with an application created mostly through AI assistance. Six months later, something breaks in production. The original founder remembers the product but does not fully understand the architecture. There are hundreds of files, several services, database relationships, authentication flows, background workers, third party integrations, and thousands of lines of generated code.

Now a senior engineer has to investigate.

Before fixing the actual problem, they may need to understand why the system was designed that way, which assumptions were made, which pieces depend on each other, what can safely be changed, and what might break somewhere else.

At that point, the money saved during the prototype stage can become much less impressive.

The issue is not that AI writes bad code all the time. It is that AI can produce a large amount of code before anyone has properly decided whether that code should exist in the first place.

The Architecture Still Matters

There is a temptation to believe that architecture is something only large companies need to worry about.

That is not really true.

A small application does not need the architecture of a global platform, but it still needs sensible boundaries. Data needs to be structured properly. Authentication needs to be handled safely. Sensitive information needs protection. Database operations need to make sense. APIs need predictable behavior. Failures need to be handled. Logs need to exist. Backups need to work.

None of this means a founder should spend six months designing infrastructure before launching.

It means the architecture should grow with the product instead of being treated as something that can be ignored forever.

AI is excellent at helping with that process when someone is actually making the decisions. It can explain architectural options, generate boilerplate, write tests, investigate errors, review code, document systems, and help refactor messy components.

The problem begins when the AI becomes the architect by default.

Vibe Coding Is Not the Enemy

I do not think vibe coding itself is the problem.

There is enormous value in being able to describe an idea and see it become software within minutes. It lowers the barrier to experimentation and gives people who are not professional programmers a way to test ideas that might otherwise remain inside a notebook.

That is a good thing.

The mistake is assuming that because AI made the first version easy, every later stage will be equally easy.

A prototype can tolerate things that production cannot. A private experiment can survive manual fixes that would be unacceptable in a customer facing product. A weekend project can run on assumptions that become dangerous when thousands of people depend on it.

The skill is knowing when the rules have changed.

AI Changes the Role of the Developer

This is where the conversation becomes more interesting.

AI does not necessarily make experienced developers less valuable. In some situations, it can make their judgment more valuable because the amount of code that can be produced is no longer the main limitation.

When writing code becomes cheaper, deciding what should be written becomes more important.

A strong developer can look at an AI generated solution and ask questions that go beyond whether the application runs. Is the data model sensible? What happens when traffic increases? What happens when this service fails? Is this authentication approach safe? Can this code be tested? Will another developer understand it six months from now? Is there a simpler way to solve the problem?

Those questions are difficult to answer with a prompt alone.

They require context.

The Prototype to Production Gap Is Getting Bigger

Ironically, AI may make the gap between prototype and production more visible.

Building a prototype has become incredibly fast. Turning that prototype into reliable production software has not suddenly become effortless.

That creates a new situation for founders.

Instead of asking whether AI can build the product, the better question is whether the team understands what AI has built well enough to operate it.

That distinction could become one of the most important technical skills of the AI era.

A founder does not need to become a world class software engineer just because AI can write code. But someone on the team needs to understand the system deeply enough to make responsible decisions about it.

Otherwise, the startup can end up moving incredibly fast in a direction nobody fully understands.

Speed Is Only Useful When You Can Survive It

The biggest advantage of AI development is speed.

The biggest risk is also speed.

When software takes months to build, there is naturally more time to think about architecture, requirements, testing, and tradeoffs. When an AI system can produce a working application over a weekend, it becomes very easy to mistake implementation speed for product progress.

Those are not the same thing.

A faster development cycle is valuable when it helps a team learn faster. Build something, put it in front of users, learn what is wrong, improve it, and repeat. That is a healthy feedback loop.

Building faster becomes dangerous when every generated feature is treated as permanent production infrastructure without understanding its consequences.

The goal should not be to slow AI down.

The goal should be to know where speed creates leverage and where it creates risk.

https://t.me/OffsecGauntlet

The Best Use of AI Is Not Blind Automation

AI coding tools are incredibly useful when they are treated as engineering partners rather than replacements for engineering judgment.

They can handle repetitive implementation work. They can generate boilerplate. They can explain unfamiliar code. They can write tests. They can suggest refactors. They can investigate bugs. They can help with documentation. They can turn rough ideas into working prototypes quickly.

That gives developers more time to focus on architecture, product decisions, reliability, security, and the parts of software development that require actual understanding.

There is a much healthier workflow here: let AI handle more of the mechanical work while humans remain responsible for the important decisions.

That is very different from asking an AI to build an entire startup and assuming the job is finished when the deployment succeeds.

The Real Advantage Goes Beyond Writing Code

The founders who benefit most from AI may not be the ones who generate the most code.

They may be the ones who learn the fastest.

AI makes it possible to test ideas cheaply, change products quickly, automate repetitive work, explore technical options, and build things that would previously have required a much larger team. That is a massive advantage when combined with good product judgment.

The important part is knowing what deserves to be built, what needs to be tested, what should remain temporary, and what needs proper engineering before customers depend on it.

That is why software engineering is not disappearing just because AI can write software.

The value is moving.

Less time may be spent manually producing every line of code. More time will be spent deciding what the system should do, checking whether the generated implementation makes sense, understanding failures, managing complexity, and taking responsibility for the result.

Build Fast, But Know What You Built

There is nothing wrong with building an MVP over a weekend.

There is nothing wrong with using Cursor, Claude, ChatGPT, or another AI coding tool to get there.

There is nothing wrong with letting AI write a large portion of the first version.

The dangerous part is forgetting that a working prototype and a reliable business are two completely different things.

AI has made the first one dramatically easier.

The second still requires engineering.

That might be the most important lesson behind the entire vibe coding conversation. The technology is not making software engineering irrelevant. It is making it possible to create software so quickly that the consequences of not understanding it can arrive much sooner.

The best founders will not be the ones who refuse to use AI.

They will be the ones who use it aggressively during experimentation, understand where its shortcuts become dangerous, and know when a quick prototype needs to become real engineering.

Because building something quickly is impressive.

Building something that keeps working when people actually depend on it is the part that matters.

A team needs its files cleaned today. Someone finds a polished utility, downloads it directly, and sees a familiar interface with one obvious function. The application removes duplicates, converts images, or prepares documents for delivery. The deadline is real. The tool appears useful.

The operating system raises a prompt. The user clicks ‘Allow’.

What exactly has been approved when a user clicks ‘Allow’?

The visible action looks small. The relationship may be large. Depending on the request, the application may gain access to files in the home directory, browser data, credentials, system settings, network services, or other resources that have little to do with the advertised feature.

macOS provides Gatekeeper, notarization, XProtect, and TCC prompts. These controls matter. They can block known threats, establish a chain of distribution, or make access requests visible. Their effect still depends on configuration, timing, and the user’s ability to understand what is happening. A prompt can expose a decision without making the decision understandable.

(A signature can establish provenance without establishing safe intent.)

Claims that AI-generated or “vibecoded” applications are already enabling widespread data theft require case-specific verification. The stronger observation concerns exposure. Software can perform its advertised task while also scanning, packaging, and transmitting unrelated data.

A utility can complete the task and still steal the workstation.

The feature is narrow. The access may not be.

Once that gap appears, the question stops being whether one suspicious application is malicious. It becomes a question about how a small decision at one workstation acquires consequences across the company.

Start with risk. The vendor controls the code. The user and employer inherit the blast radius.

A compromised utility, malicious feature, compromised dependency, or careless AI-generated application can expose documents, browser sessions, wallet files, credentials, or proprietary material. Whether any particular application did so requires evidence. The structural possibility requires less investigation. If software can reach data unrelated to its stated purpose, the company has accepted a relationship it may not understand.

The user who approves access becomes the visible decision-maker. The employer pays for the investigation, lost work, customer notification, legal review, recovery, and reputational damage. The click is individual; the liability is organizational.

The prompt appears on one person’s screen. The machine may belong to an employee, while the data belongs to customers, colleagues, or the company. The operating system presents a local choice and leaves the consequences to a much larger system.

The incentives point in different directions. Developers are rewarded for shipping polished features quickly. Users are rewarded for removing friction from an immediate task. Managers are rewarded for visible speed and output. Security is rewarded only when nothing happens, so its objections look expensive until the event it prevented becomes visible.

The person at the keyboard experiences the deadline. Security experiences the unresolved questions. Management experiences pressure for results. The vendor experiences adoption. The distribution of value and risk is uneven before anyone opens the application.

A cleaner, converter, or image tool produces a useful result, but it also represents an access path into the workstation and possibly into the organization. Its value cannot be measured only in hours saved. The permissions create another relationship with company data, often without the review applied to enterprise software, formal vendors, or managed integrations.

Polished interface, unpriced access.

A product team may see a small utility. An attacker, or a careless developer, may see a route to browser sessions, documents, credentials, and internal systems. The user sees a task completed. Procurement may see no vendor contract. Security may see an unmanaged binary with an unknown update path. All of these descriptions can be accurate at the same time.

A legitimate feature can obtain trust for a different purpose. A file-cleaning tool asks for access to a broad set of files, and that access supplies an opportunity to collect unrelated data. An image application requests network access, and the same channel could transmit material beyond the images being processed. The application does not need to be proven malicious for the arrangement to deserve scrutiny.

Using a legitimate feature to obtain trust and access for unrelated data collection is permission laundering.

The label belongs only where the elements can be identified: a real feature, access broader than that feature requires, and a plausible risk of unrelated collection. A tool can request excessive permissions through ignorance, haste, or bad defaults. The governance problem remains when intent is uncertain.

Policy often becomes the response. Direct downloads are prohibited. The user sees a deadline. The team still needs the files cleaned today. Policy has described preferred behavior without changing the conditions producing the shortcut.

“Just install it; we need the files cleaned today” Sales says.

IT asks who reviewed the binary, what permissions it needs, and where the data goes. Product answers that the tool saves hours and that the customer already approved access. Security blocks it. The team downloads it anyway, outside the approved channel, because the deadline measures output, not exposure.

This is an operating pattern, and morality explains little of it. The user may be acting reasonably with the information available. Security may be acting reasonably within its duty to protect the company. Product may be reporting a genuine loss caused by a slow process. The failure sits between those positions.

If nothing happens, the shortcut becomes precedent. The application remains installed. Someone else uses it later. Its permissions survive the original task. The exception becomes part of the software inventory without ever being entered into one.

If something happens, the user gets blamed for clicking Allow. Management asks why Security slowed the business. The deadline disappears from the story, along with the missing review, the unexamined permission request, and the lack of a safe alternative.

Who benefits from treating the download as a user decision?

The arrangement lets the organization externalize accountability onto the person at the keyboard. The user supplies the consent that makes access socially acceptable. The employer retains the data, the legal obligations, and the recovery bill.

Technical details complicate the picture. Open-source visibility helps when somebody audits the code and verifies that the shipped binary matches it. A public repository by itself establishes very little. A signed or notarized application may have passed an integrity or distribution check while still behaving in ways the user did not expect after launch.

Browser cookies may carry more immediate value than passwords in some attacks, but that claim depends on the application, browser protections, session design, and the specific data exposed. Legitimate shell tools and network utilities can support data movement that basic signature scanning does not recognize as suspicious. Sandboxing can reduce an application’s reach while leaving room for permission abuse, social engineering, or a user granting access that defeats the intended boundary.

“Open Anyway” converts a warning into a user decision, not a security control.

Users approve permissions every day. Routine approval can be reasonable when the requested access is narrow and expected. It does not establish informed approval. The relevant questions are whether the access is necessary for the stated task, where the data will go, how long it will be retained, and whether anyone can reconstruct the decision later.

A person under deadline pressure may not distinguish access to one selected folder from access to a home directory. They may not know what browser data can reveal, whether the tool sends files to a vendor service, or whether the service retains them for diagnostics or model training. The prompt rarely answers these questions.

Notarization deserves the same careful treatment. It helps establish that an application passed a review process associated with its developer identity and distribution. It does not certify that the application’s behavior matches the user’s interests. Delivery trust and behavioral trust are different problems.

What would blocking direct downloads solve?

It could reduce exposure. It could also move the same decision to a shell command, an unmanaged machine, a personal account, a browser-based service, or an exception granted in private. When the work still has to be completed, a hard block may remove visibility without removing demand.

Then the record disappears.

Nobody can answer what the application accessed, where it sent data, which version ran, who approved it, or whether it remains installed. The company has created a software dependency it cannot inspect or govern.

The first practical move is to classify the request by access, not by product category. “Cleaner”, “converter” and “image tool” describe the marketing surface. They say little about the relationship the application wants with the machine:

  • Does it need one selected folder or the whole home directory?
  • Does it touch browser data, credentials, wallet files, system controls, or network destinations?
  • Does the task require an external service?
  • Does the application create persistent background processes?
  • Does it update itself from a source the company cannot verify?

The name should carry less weight than the permission boundary.

This also changes the conversation with users. An employee asking for a utility may be accepting the default because the software presents no narrower option. The review should test whether the task can be completed with selected inputs, a disposable account, a copy of the data, or an environment separated from ordinary work.

The second move is a short, visible exception path that preserves urgency while forcing ownership. The request should record the binary or version, requested permissions, stated purpose, data destination, approving person, and expiration date.

That is not paperwork for its own sake. It prevents a temporary shortcut from becoming invisible permanent inventory and gives the user a route that does not require pretending the deadline is imaginary.

The company builds a fast side entrance, then discovers it connects directly to the vault.

The safer path must be faster than the bypass. A controlled test machine may be enough for one utility. A disposable account may limit the data exposed. A sandboxed environment, restricted network access, or preapproved catalogue may handle recurring needs. These controls work when they are available at the moment of pressure, rather than described in a policy document nobody can consult during the deadline.

(The goal is controlled urgency, not a ceremonial approval process.)

A prompt asking a user to make a high-stakes judgment with incomplete information is a weak control. Give the user a safe place to test the tool. Limit the files available to it. Record the version. Restrict outbound connections where practical. Remove access when the task ends.

The organization also needs to measure what it currently hides. Security teams should know how many requests were approved, rejected, expired, or bypassed. Product and management should see the time saved alongside the access granted and the remaining exposure. Users need a route for reporting that the approved process cannot meet the deadline without being treated as the problem.

This produces an uncomfortable form of speed. The organization moves quickly when a tool has narrow permissions and a controlled test path. It slows down when one feature requests broad access to sensitive data.

The pause separates the useful task from the unpriced dependency.

[ ]_Could the files be cleaned without giving the utility access to unrelated folders?
[ ]_Could the conversion happen on a controlled machine?
[ ]_Could the network be disabled until the result is verified?
[ ]_Could the data be copied into a temporary workspace and deleted afterward?

These questions are more useful than asking whether the application feels trustworthy. The answer may still be yes. Someone has examined the relationship.

The vendor writes the code. The developer controls the release. The user clicks the approval. The manager owns the deadline. Security owns the objection. The employer absorbs the incident.

These roles look separate until an application crosses the workstation boundary. Then they form a chain of control without a single accountable owner. The vendor can change the application. The user may grant a new permission. The manager may demand an exception. Security may lack the telemetry to see what happened. The employer remains responsible for the result.

AI-assisted development makes polished utilities easier to produce and distribute. Direct downloads make them easier to adopt. Operating-system protections make some risks visible, but they do not decide who should evaluate the permission or who should bear the consequence. A company can allow a private decision at a workstation to carry public organizational consequences.

Permission laundering names a power relationship as much as a software pattern. A legitimate feature supplies the social permission. Broad access supplies the technical reach. The user supplies the visible consent. The organization supplies the data, liability, and recovery effort.

The user opens one service door and hands the visitor a master key.

Often, the user does this under a deadline created elsewhere, in response to a prompt designed by the operating system, with limited information about what the key can open. The visible approval therefore becomes a kind of organizational handoff. Control has been distributed across people who can each influence the decision, while authority to absorb the consequences remains concentrated in the company.

The deeper question is who gets to decide when convenience becomes access, and who gets to decline the cost when that access goes wrong.

When speed makes the user approve access and the organization absorb the damage, who actually controls the machine?

medium.titulo: Build a Beautiful Website with Just Prompts: Claude + Inspyry, From Blank Page to Lighthouse 99
medium.resumo: You do not need to write code, open a design tool or hire an illustrator to get a website that looks designed. You need a handful of…
medium.conteudo_html:
You do not need to write code, open a design tool or hire an illustrator to get a website that looks designed. You need a handful of plain-English prompts, an AI agent such as Claude, and one extra tool that can draw.

This post walks through exactly that. I built a landing page for a made-up coffee subscription called Moss & Mug by describing what I wanted, step by step. Claude wrote the page. Inspyry drew the brand: a logo, icons, a mascot and a badge, all as SVG. Then I asked for a performance audit and a round of fixes.

The first draft scored 77 for performance in Lighthouse, with a 4.2 second largest contentful paint. After the fixes it scored 99 with 1.9 seconds. Every number below comes from a real run, and every image is a real output. For each step I give you the prompt in plain words, what came back, and what to watch for.

What you need

  • An AI agent that can use skills or MCP servers. I used Claude Code. Other coding agents that run commands should work with the same prompts, but I only tested Claude.
  • The Inspyry vector skill. It is an open-source Agent Skill that lets the agent turn a text prompt into a flat-colour SVG. You can ask your agent to install it from that repository. Inspyry also hosts an MCP server at inspyry.com/mcp if your agent prefers that route.
  • An Inspyry API key, stored as the INSPYRY_API_KEY environment variable or in a .env file. Never paste it into a prompt. A request made with a key carries a commercial licence, while the free keyless allowance is personal use only.

Why it matters: the agent can only use tools you have given it. Claude writes pages well but does not draw, so the skill fills the one gap that otherwise leaves every AI-built page looking like a template.

Prompt 1: Start with a brief, not a wish

A vague request gets a generic page. A good first prompt names the product, the audience, the constraints and a measurable goal:

Plan a single-page website for Moss & Mug, a monthly small-batch coffee subscription for people who brew at home. Calm, friendly tone. Palette: moss green #2f4a3a, clay #c8793a, oat #f3e9d8. Use only SVG artwork we generate together, with no stock photos and no placeholder boxes. The goal is Lighthouse mobile scores of 95 or higher for performance, and 100 for accessibility, best practices and SEO. Ask me anything unclear before you start.

The last two sentences do the most work. A target Claude can measure turns “make it good” into a task with a pass or fail, and the invitation to ask questions stops it guessing.

Prompt 2: Generate a matching brand kit

Using the Inspyry skill, make a brand kit: a logo of a steaming coffee mug, three simple line icons (a coffee bean, a pour-over kettle, a delivery box), a sleepy red panda mascot hugging a mug, and a round roaster’s seal with a coffee branch. Use my palette for every image so they match. Save each as an SVG, then show me a contact sheet. Do not regenerate anything I have approved.

Here is what came back:

Inspyry gives you controls for style, shape and colour count, and the skill uses them for you. Behind this prompt the agent picked a minimal style for the logo, a line style for the icons, a kawaii style for the mascot and an engraved wreath for the seal. Passing the same three colours to every request is what makes six separate generations look like one brand.

Prompt 3: Ask for a plan, then the page

Now build the page using only the files we just made. Before writing any code, give me a short design plan: colours, fonts, layout, and why they suit a coffee subscription. Then build it as a single HTML file, make it work on a phone, and check it with screenshots before you show me.

Asking for a plan first gets you a deliberate design rather than a default one. Claude chose a heavy grotesque for headlines and a book serif for body text. It placed the mascot in the hero with the seal rotated over its shoulder like a stamp, turned the three icons into a step-by-step band, and styled the pricing like a café menu board with dotted lines to the prices.

On a phone the layout collapses to one column with the mascot above the headline:

It looks finished. That is exactly when to check.

Prompt 4: Make the agent measure, not just look

Run Lighthouse on this page three times with the mobile preset and report the median for each category. List every failing check before you change anything.

This is the prompt most people skip, and it is the most useful one. A screenshot cannot show you load time, missing metadata or oversized files. Here is what the first draft scored:

  • Performance: 77
  • Accessibility: 100
  • Best practices: 96
  • SEO: 91
  • Largest contentful paint: 4.21 seconds
  • Layout shift: 0

Accessibility was already perfect, a fair credit to the markup Claude wrote: real headings, alt text and sufficient contrast. The weak spots were performance and SEO. I did not read the full report line by line, but the page had no meta description and no favicon, and its favicon request returned a 404. These are lab numbers from a local server, so a deployed site will differ.

Why it matters: the audit is what lets the agent improve its own work. Without a number to beat, it can only agree that the page looks fine.

Prompt 5: Harden the site

Fix what the audit found, in this order, and re-run Lighthouse after each group so we can see what helped: (1) shrink the SVG files without changing how they look, and prove it by comparing before and after renders; (2) add a favicon, an Apple touch icon and a 1200x630 social share image made from our SVGs, without generating anything new; (3) add a meta description, Open Graph tags and image dimensions; (4) add a robots file.

Claude did all four. I will be upfront about one thing: in my run the changes went in together, so I cannot say which one moved which number. Asking for a re-run after each group, as the prompt above does, fixes that.

What came back:

  • Smaller SVGs. Total artwork fell from 248 KB to 154 KB, a 38 percent saving, with no visible change. Claude rendered every file before and after in Chrome and compared pixels, and zero pixels changed in all six. Flat-colour SVG is not automatically tiny, though. The engraved seal started at 146 KB and the mascot at 62 KB, so the style you ask for affects the page budget.
  • Icons and share card from the same art. I checked that the logo stayed readable at 16 and 32 pixels, so no new generation was needed. One set of vector files produced the favicon, the touch icon and this share card, with no credits spent.

The final audit, same method as before:

  • Performance: 77 to 99
  • Accessibility: 100 to 100
  • Best practices: 96 to 100
  • SEO: 91 to 100
  • Largest contentful paint: 4.21 to 1.88 seconds
  • Layout shift: 0 to 0

The page still weighs 436 KB. A quick network capture shows about 266 KB of that is web fonts, which is more than all the artwork combined. Self-hosting the fonts is the obvious next prompt, and I have not done it.

What each piece actually did

Claude wrote the design plan, the HTML and CSS, the metadata and the fixes. Its markup earned the perfect accessibility score from the first draft.

Inspyry supplied the brand artwork: six consistent SVG files for about ten credits, including a few throwaway tries, with a commercial licence on every request. It did not write copy, build the layout or move the Lighthouse scores. Those came from Claude’s build and hardening work.

You supplied the brief, the palette, the approval of each asset and the measurable goal. That is the part nobody can prompt away.

Tips for better prompts

  • Fix the palette first and repeat it in every request.
  • Constrain the imagery. Saying “only our SVGs” stops the agent from reaching for stock photos.
  • Ask for a plan before code. It gets you a design instead of a default.
  • Give a number to beat. Lighthouse targets make the agent check its own work.
  • Approve before moving on, and tell the agent not to redo approved assets.
  • Change one group of things at a time, and ask for a re-measure after each.

Key takeaways

  • A beautiful, fast website needs five prompts: a brief, a brand kit, a page, an audit and a hardening pass.
  • Claude builds the page, and a skill such as Inspyry’s draws what Claude cannot.
  • A measurable goal is what separates a demo from something you can ship.
  • Agents that spend credits need a rule against rerunning approved steps.
  • Measure before and after, and be clear about which tool earned which result.

What’s next

This was a side trip from the main roadmap, showing how AI tooling fits into real product work. Next on the main track is chain rule and backpropagation by hand, which is how gradients are computed for networks with millions of parameters.

This is part of a roadmap from basic maths to deploying AI systems. Previously: Derivatives and Gradients from Scratch, NumPy Matrix Operations and Singular Value Decomposition. Code is the best teacher, so run every example yourself.

medium.titulo: I Denied Read(.env). Six of the Ten Claude Code Mods I Loaded Could Still Read It.
medium.resumo: Claude Code mods run inside the agent with your permissions and no sandbox. I built an admission gate in Swift to work out what a lead…
medium.conteudo_html:
Claude Code mods run inside the agent with your permissions and no sandbox. I built an admission gate in Swift to work out what a lead should allow, pin and refuse.

Claude Code mods shipped on 1 October. Within a day, someone had Tetris running inside the agent. Security researchers at Pluto Security then showed a mod quietly reading a credentials file and sending it out, according to byteiota’s launch write-up. Both work for the same reason. A Claude Code mod is a JavaScript or TypeScript module that runs inside the agent, with your permissions, and nothing sandboxes it.

My first instinct was the one I suspect most leads had: write a Read(.env) deny rule and move on. Then I read the admin docs properly, and that instinct turned out to be wrong in a specific, testable way.

A mod sits inside the agent loop

Settings hooks run a command, an HTTP call, a prompt or an agent when something happens. A mod sits in the middle of the agent. It exports register(on) and subscribes to events such as tool.call, prompt.submit and tool.check. Each handler gets the event and a next continuation, so it can watch, rewrite the payload, or return a denial without calling next at all. The docs say mods need Claude Code v2.1.287 or later and are on by default.

That middleware shape is what makes them useful. An iOS team can collapse a wall of xcodebuild output to the first real error, or add booted-simulator state to every prompt. It's also what makes them a governance problem. A mod that sees every tool call can change every tool call.

The guard protects what you manage. It doesn’t vet what your team installs

Claude Code ships a built-in guard, sec-default@builtin. It loads ahead of every user's mod when the machine has managed settings or the user is on a Team or Enterprise plan. It stops a user's mod from tampering with your managed hooks, the system prompt, your managed CLAUDE.md and your managed MCP servers. Where it loads, a mod also can't approve a tool call that a deny rule refuses.

Then the admin docs say the part that matters. Deny rules and managed PreToolUse hooks apply to Claude's tool calls. They don't apply to a mod's own $.fs and $.process calls. In the docs' words, "with Read(.env) denied, a mod can still read that file with $.fs.read."

A deny rule is a promise about Claude’s tool calls. It was never a promise about the code running next to Claude.

I built the admission gate in Swift to see the size of the gap

The demo is a Swift package, ModAdmission, with an iOS app that runs on the Simulator. It parses the hooks: and calls: lines that claude plugin validate prints. It works out each mod's tier from where the mod was installed, and gives each mod a blast radius. Mods that write files, run programs or change the environment are machine. Mods that rewrite or decide, read files or secrets, touch the network or speak as the user are session. Everything else is contained.

I fed it a constructed registry of eleven mods, the kind an iOS team writes in week one. It isn’t a survey of real plugins. The set includes a build-log digester, a simulator-state injector, a Jira context fetcher, a status-line token counter, an auto-approver for swiftformat, and one mod Claude wrote mid-session.

My baseline is a Team plan with the guard loaded and a policy mod built the same way as the docs’ first example, but with an empty block list and no .catch. Under it, 10 of the 11 load, one of them unchecked because its check timed out. The only refusal is a mod whose API use the validator can't read, which Claude Code refuses anyway. Six of those ten can still reach .env. Four read files with $.fs.read, three start programs that could read it, and one does both. On a personal plan with no managed settings, the guard doesn't load and the swiftformat auto-approver makes it seven, because now it can approve the denied Read call.

Three lines in the docs I’d have got wrong

Managed doesn’t mean yours. A mod counts as your organization’s only if three things hold: managed enabledPlugins turns it on, its marketplace is a directory on the machine given by absolute path, and the plugin loads in place. Enable a plugin from GitHub in managed settings and it still runs as a user's mod. In my registry, pr-template@acme-github is exactly that.

Your policy check fails open. If your plugin.register hook throws or runs past its time limit, Claude Code skips it and the mod loads. My snapshot-diff mod gets through unchecked by default. The docs show a .catch handler that refuses instead. Use it.

One list can delete the guard. Setting prependPlugins in managed settings replaces the default order. If the list doesn't name sec-default@builtin, the guard doesn't load, and allowManagedModsOnly stops doing anything. There's a test in the repo for that case.

The policy I’d actually ship

public static let lead = TeamPolicy(
    blockedCalls: [ModCall("process.spawn"), ModCall("env.set")],
    failClosed: true,          // a check that throws or times out refuses
    requirePins: true,         // SHA-256 of the reviewed code, per mod
    reviewAtOrAbove: .machine  // machine-radius mods need a reviewed pin
)

I leave $.process.run unblocked because the build digester needs it. The machine-radius rule forces a reviewed pin on it instead. Under that policy, 4 mods load, 4 are held and 3 are refused. The held mods include sim-state, which had a reviewed pin at v4 and now ships v5. A silent update doesn't ride in on an old yes. Only two loaded mods can still reach .env: the platform team's own redactor, and the build digester someone actually reviewed.

Once mods exist, “the team’s agent” is a product with an owner, a release process and a review queue. The same goes for any language your team writes in. Somebody has to own that queue, and if nobody’s name is on it, the default policy is “everything a curious engineer installs at 11pm”.

If this changes what you’ll check before your team’s first mod goes in, a clap helps it reach other leads making the same call. You can give up to 50.

And one question I’d like real answers to: which mod would your team refuse first, the one that runs programs or the one that quietly approves tool calls?

Sources: Claude Code docs, Manage mods for your organization and Mods overview; launch coverage from AlphaSignal and byteiota. Demo repo: claude-code-mod-admission-article-demo.
